109.0.s.en: (1) The hatred of the wicked for the righteous

109.0.0.en: 1- Hold not thy peace, O God of my praise, 2- For the mouth of the wicked and the mouth of the deceitful are opened against me: they have spoken against me with a lying tongue. 3- They compassed me about also with words of hatred; and fought against me without a cause.

109.0.1.en: 1- David was accustomed to prayer every day and to praising God, even when troubles came upon him, because his life was prayer. But here he asks God to intervene to rescue him from the affliction through which he is passing, for Ahithophel counseled Absalom and helped him to kill his father David.

109.0.2.en: 2- David describes his enemies with three characteristics: wickedness, deceit and lying. All this expresses their hatred of him, although he had not wronged them.

109.0.3.en: 3- These verses are a prophecy about Christ, the only-begotten Son, whose life is prayer and continual conversation with the Father, and who at the same time faced betrayal by His disciple Judas, the fury of His Jewish nation against Him, and the hatred of the priests, the scribes and the Pharisees for Him, together with their wickedness, their deceit and their lying, by which they tried many times to trap Him in a word but were unable; so they fabricated many charges against Him, and in the end they crucified Him unjustly.

109.1.0.en: 4- For my love they are my adversaries: but I give myself unto prayer. 5- And they have rewarded me evil for good, and hatred for my love.

109.1.1.en: 1- David loved all those around him, even those who were hostile to him, such as Saul. But the wicked rose up against him, not only Saul and those with him, but also his son Absalom and David's counselor Ahithophel. They repaid David's love with betrayal and evil, and this shows how deeply they were immersed in evil, for they hated him though they knew that he was innocent and loved them. On the other hand, David continued to love them and to pray for them always; therefore he said, "but I give myself unto prayer."

109.1.2.en: 2- These two verses are a prophecy about Christ, who loved His disciples and all the multitudes, worked many miracles with them, and cared for them with varied teachings. But they rose up against Him with the help and betrayal of His disciple Judas Iscariot, while Christ continued to pray for them and to warn Judas to turn back from his evil.

109.1.3.en: May you look to the love of Christ, so that you learn love and become accustomed to it in all your relationships. And if anyone wrongs you, continue to pray for him and love him, that perhaps he may repent, so that you continue throughout your life in prayer, praise and love.

109.2.0.en: "Set thou a wicked man over him: and let Satan stand at his right hand." The wicked one whom God sets over him is Satan, who stands at his right hand; that is, the wicked man receives his strength from him, because the right hand represents strength. These words are a prophecy of what would happen to Ahithophel, David's counselor, or to the Jewish nation, or to Judas Iscariot. The right hand of the spiritual man is in God's hand, as it was with David (Ps 16:8). But if a man rejects God and persists in rejecting Him, Satan takes God's place, because God forsakes him and hands him over to Satan, who takes his strength and his gifts. Judas was a disciple close to Christ; he went out with the disciples, healed the sick and cast out demons, and saw at close range the works of Christ and heard His words; then Satan came to be at his right hand, because he rejected God, and Satan became his adversary, tormented him and led him to suicide.

109.3.0.en: "When he shall be judged, let him be condemned: and let his prayer become sin."

109.3.1.en: 1- David continues his prophecy about Ahithophel, or the Jewish nation, or Judas Iscariot, and declares that if he comes forward for trial on the day of judgment he will be found guilty and will be punished with eternal perdition. And if he cries out to God at that time, his prayer will not be accepted, because the time has passed.

109.3.2.en: 2- If this wicked man, in his life, judges himself before his conscience, he will discover that he is guilty. And if he prays while persisting in sin, he gains nothing from his prayer. As for Judas, when he repented after betraying Christ, his remorse appears to be prayer, but it was despair, and it led him to hang himself.

109.4.0.en: "Let his days be few; and let another take his office."

109.4.1.en: 1- David prophesies about this traitor that the days of his life will be short; for Ahithophel and Judas each hanged himself (2 Sam 17:23; Mt 27:5), and the Jewish nation was destroyed by the Roman Titus in AD 70, when he laid Jerusalem waste and killed a million and a half of the Jews.

109.4.2.en: 2- The office of this wicked man was a great office, which another takes. In place of Ahithophel came Hushai the Archite (2 Sam 17:14), and in place of Judas Iscariot came the Apostle Matthias (Acts 1:

109.4.3.en: 26), and in place of the Jewish nation came the Church of the New Testament, which has spread everywhere.

109.5.0.en: 9- Let his children be fatherless, and his wife a widow. 10- Let his children be continually vagabonds, and beg: let them seek their bread also out of their desolate places. 11- Let the extortioner catch all that he hath; and let the strangers spoil his labour. 12- Let there be none to extend mercy unto him: neither let there be any to favour his fatherless children. 13- Let his posterity be cut off; and in the generation following let their name be blotted out. 14- Let the iniquity of his fathers be remembered with the LORD; and let not the sin of his mother be blotted out. 15- Let them be before the LORD continually, that he may cut off the memory of them from the earth.

109.5.1.en: 1- Evil and ruin come upon the followers of this wicked man, although no source mentions that Judas Iscariot had a wife or children. But if he had a wife and children who walked in evil, having learned it from him, all these curses come upon them, so that his wife becomes a widow, because Judas hanged himself, and his children become orphans through the death of their father. His sons become poor and so beg, and ruin comes upon them. The extortioner who catches their labor is Satan, and the strangers are the demons. No one has mercy on his offspring or shows them kindness, because they are wicked. His offspring die, and no one is left to perpetuate his memory. And his wicked parents, who taught him evil, are punished.

109.5.2.en: 2- If Judas had no wife and children, then his offspring are his deeds and his thoughts, or all who walk in evil as he did, and so all the curses mentioned before come upon him. This applies also to Ahithophel.

109.5.3.en: 3- And if we apply this to the Jewish nation, then the extortioner and the strangers are Titus and the Roman soldiers, who destroyed Jerusalem and killed the Jews, and everyone who has persecuted the Jews throughout the generations, such as Hitler the German.

109.6.0.en: 16- Because that he remembered not to shew mercy, but persecuted the poor and needy man, that he might even slay the broken in heart. 17- As he loved cursing, so let it come unto him: as he delighted not in blessing, so let it be far from him. 18- As he clothed himself with cursing like as with his garment, so let it come into his bowels like water, and like oil into his bones. 19- Let it be unto him as the garment which covereth him, and for a girdle wherewith he is girded continually. 20- Let this be the reward of mine adversaries from the LORD, and of them that speak evil against my soul.

109.6.1.en: The cause of all the calamities and curses that may come upon the wicked man is his oppression of the poor and needy and his depriving them of all strength or help; this means Christ, or David. So did Judas, or Ahithophel, or the Jewish nation. So the curses which they desired came upon them, because they desired evil. And evil is joined to cursing, so they put on evil like a garment, indeed they put it on also as an outer robe like a cloak, and girded themselves with it, that is, they braced themselves to do evil. So it entered into their bowels and their bones, that is, they held fast to evil from within, which is their thoughts and feelings, and from without, which is their deeds. And the curse came upon them, that is, they were tormented within and without, and nothing awaits them in the end but eternal torment. This is the reward of him who clings to evil, so that it becomes part of his nature and it is very difficult for him to leave it; even if his inner being is pained by turmoil and anxiety, he rejects the voice of God and persists in evil until death, as Judas and Ahithophel each hanged himself; for they loved evil, so the curse came upon them, which is the inevitable result of evil, and consequently the blessing of God was far from them, for they rejected Him by their own will and did not love Him. Ahithophel rejected his great position as David's counselor, and Judas rejected the greatest thing, which was his discipleship to Christ and his apostleship.

109.6.2.en: Do not be careless and accept evil, even if it is small, lest it creep into your inner being and the devil deceive you, so that you love it and it gradually gains mastery over you, until you can no longer hear the voice of God, and you continue to drift away from Him and lose your life.

109.7.0.en: 21- But do thou for me, O GOD the Lord, for thy name's sake: because thy mercy is good, deliver thou me. 22- For I am poor and needy, and my heart is wounded within me.

109.7.1.en: 1- Although David spoke by the spirit of prophecy about what would happen to Ahithophel, or to Judas Iscariot, he is not occupied with evil and its recompense, but comes humbly before God and prays, asking for mercy and deliverance from the hand of the wicked. Two things appear in David's prayer:

109.7.2.en: a - His humility, for he says "for thy name's sake," and describes himself as poor and needy, and wounded within.

109.7.3.en: b - His faith in the merciful God, who is able to deliver him.

109.7.4.en: 2- These two verses are a prophecy about the sufferings of Christ and His cross, because David is a type of Christ. Christ speaks as the Son of Man, that is, on behalf of humanity, and He speaks to the Father, asking for mercy and deliverance; for in His human form He is poor and needy and His heart is wounded, because He will bear all the sins of the world upon Himself, and everyone has forsaken Him, and His disciple has betrayed Him, and He will endure all the torments for the sake of our salvation. So He asks for the Father's help and mercy in His sufferings, as He expressed the harshness of the sufferings by saying in the garden of Gethsemane, "remove this cup from me" (Lk 22:42).

109.8.0.en: 23- I am gone like the shadow when it declineth: I am tossed up and down as the locust. 24- My knees are weak through fasting; and my flesh faileth of fatness. 25- I became also a reproach unto them: when they looked upon me they shaked their heads.

109.8.1.en: "Shaked": they shook their heads in mockery and scorn.

109.8.2.en: 1- David likens his life, with all the hardships he endured, to a shadow, short and passing; indeed David died at the age of seventy. He likens himself also to a locust, a light insect that is tossed about before the wind that carries it. So David too suffered in his soul, as if he were trembling within.

109.8.3.en: David also declares that he took refuge in God with many fasts, and that he ate vegetable food cooked with oil. From the many fasts his body grew weak and his knees trembled, and his body, which had been full and fat, became lean and thin, so that his enemies mocked him, and he became an example of shame and ridicule. David mentions all this to show his weakness with humility before God, asking for His help.

109.8.4.en: 2- These verses are a prophecy about Christ, who appeared in the flesh as weak as a locust and trembled in His soul from the multitude of sufferings; His life passed swiftly, and He died young, at about thirty-three years of age. His body grew weak and became lean from the fasts, and also from the sufferings and the scourging, and He became an example of shame when He was hung on the cross, and the Jews mocked Him and shook their heads (Mt 27:39; Mk 15:29). All this He bore for our sake, and He asks the Father's help to complete the redemption.

109.9.0.en: 26- Help me, O LORD my God: O save me according to thy mercy: 27- That they may know that this is thy hand; that thou, LORD, hast done it.

109.9.1.en: 1- David asks for God's help according to His abundant mercy, for he trusts in God's limitless mercy. And when his enemies see God's power which protects him, they will learn the importance of walking in righteousness and of God's care for the righteous, that perhaps they may repent of their evil and return to God.

109.9.2.en: 2- These two verses also are a prophecy about Christ, who speaks in the voice of humanity as He approaches the sufferings of the cross, and asks for the Father's help and mercy, so that those who persecute Him may know that He is the Son of God, the awaited Messiah, so that they may believe in Him and understand that the sufferings and the crucifixion are God's will for the salvation of humanity.

109.10.0.en: 28- Let them curse, but bless thou: when they arise, let them be ashamed; but let thy servant rejoice.

109.10.1.en: 29- Let mine adversaries be clothed with shame, and let them cover themselves with their own confusion, as with a mantle.

109.10.2.en: 1- David declares that his enemies curse him while he blesses them, as Saul and Absalom did to him, whereas he forgave Saul and had compassion on his son Absalom. So he was in peace and joy with God because of his love. And perhaps God's dealing with David and His protection of him will shame his enemies, so that they are abashed and put to shame, that perhaps by this they may repent. For David did not ask for their destruction, but only for their shame, that they might turn back from their evil.

109.10.3.en: 2- The Jews persecuted Christ and tried many times to kill Him; then they seized Him, tortured Him and crucified Him, whereas He cared for them, healed their sick and fed them. And when they had completed all their evil by crucifying Him, they were put to shame when they saw that He had risen from the dead. Perhaps this would have led them to repent and believe in Him, but they were put to shame because of their evil, while He was in joy for the accomplishment of redemption on the cross: they hate Him, and He loves them and dies for them.

109.11.0.en: 30- I will greatly praise the LORD with my mouth; yea, I will praise him among the multitude. 31- For he shall stand at the right hand of the poor, to save him from those that condemn his soul.

109.11.1.en: 1- At the close of the psalm David thanks God and praises Him, not only in his chamber but in the midst of the congregation of the Jews during the worship of God, because God stood by his side and delivered him from the hand of Saul and Absalom and all his enemies.

109.11.2.en: 2- Christ, by His death and His redemption of humanity, offers through the sacrifice of Himself the greatest praise before the Father, and as the Son of Man He thanks Him because He stood by His side, and triumphed over all the demons who were trying to stop the redemption.

109.11.3.en: Therefore the Church, which is the mouth of God on earth, praises God always for His care and His love.

109.11.4.en: And if, for a wicked man like Judas, Satan stands at his right hand, here we find the Father standing beside the Son, and Christ standing beside every believer who suffers hardships on earth.

109.11.5.en: Be sure that God is beside you when sufferings surround you, even if all those around you rise up against you. Know that God is stronger than all, and able to deliver you from their hands, so that your heart is filled with joy and praise, while they are put to shame, that perhaps they may repent.

109.11.6.en: Christ, the victor on behalf of David. Psalm "The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand) "..(v. 1) Introduction:

109.11.7.en: 1- Its author: the prophet David, as the title of the psalm states, and as Christ declared in the New Testament (Mt 22:44).

109.11.8.en: 2- When was it written? After David's victories over the nations surrounding him.

109.11.9.en: 3- This psalm is one of the greatest Messianic psalms, because it speaks entirely of the awaited Messiah, and the Jews agree on this, as appears from Christ's words with them (Mt 22:41-46).

109.11.10.en: 4- The psalm tells us of the attributes of Christ: He is the Lord, the King, the Priest, the Judge, and the Conqueror of His enemies.

109.11.11.en: 5- This psalm was sung at the coronation of the kings of the kingdom of Judah, that is, the kings who were of the seed of David.

109.11.12.en: 6- This psalm is among the psalms most quoted by the New Testament: Christ Himself used it (Mk 12:35-37), Peter mentioned it in his sermon on the day of Pentecost (Acts 2:34), and the Apostle Paul drew on it in his epistles to the Corinthians and the Hebrews (1 Cor 15:

109.11.14.en: 7- This psalm is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of the Ninth Hour, because in it Christ appeared triumphant over Satan; for He paid the debt by His death and bound Satan by the sacrifice of Himself, for He is the Great High Priest.
